newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Nickel industry growth seen assuring cobalt supply.
newsitem.headline: Nickel industry growth seen assuring cobalt supply.

text.p: Future supplies of cobalt will be heavily influenced by the nickel industry, which looked set to expand, Martyn Day, president of the International Cobalt Company Inc, told a conference in Hong Kong on Thursday.

"The cobalt business is unlikely to find itself short of cobalt and should regard the Western nickel industry, a non-discretionary producer, a secure source and a reliable supplier of cobalt," Day said.

The nickel industry accounted for 11,570 tonnes of 1996 cobalt production from primary sources, with 8,070 tonnes from the Western industry and 3,500 tonnes from the Eastern industry, mostly Russia, Day said in his presentation.
If secondary sources were included, nickel accounted for 12,870 tonnes of world production, he said.
Day estimated total world production of cobalt in 1996 at 29,130 tonnes. He was addressing a meeting organised by the Cobalt Development Institute in Hong Kong.
"Clearly if we seek clarification of possible cobalt supply changes, we should look to the nickel industry," Day said.

Cobalt has to be co-produced in order to make London Metal Exchange (LME) warrantable nickel, he said, adding this was not necessarily the case for copper production, where cobalt recovery was discretionary.

"Western supply capacity for nickel should increase by 205,000 tonnes to 888,000 tonnes in the year 2000 and this will be accompagnied by an increase in capacity for co-production of cobalt of 8,020 tonnes," Day said.
"I have identified Voisey's Bay as a probable producer adding 125,000 tonnes of nickel and some 3,000 tonnes of cobalt to the market when it reaches full production," Day added.
He noted that concentrates could start appearing as early as 1999, though a date after the year 2000 seemed more likely.
Voisey's Bay is a huge nickel deposit in northern Canada.
Day estimated that secondary sources and releases from the U.S. Defense Logistics Agency (DLA) stockpile added a further 6,660 tonnes to 1996 production numbers.

"If these sources maintain their output with no increases, adding the (increased) production from the Western nickel industry could result in the potential availability of about 37,000 tonnes of cobalt in the year 2000 and 40,000 tonnes when Voisey's Bay reaches capacity," Day said.

Day cautioned the industry should adjust numbers downwards for double accounting and then anticipate that when supply exceeded demand, prices would drop and result in the curtailment of more expensive production.
